Я выбираю кандидата 3. Это оценка в уме, а не полная пошаговая симуляция.

**Постоянные затраты на заказы.** Каждый день, в который что-то заказано, стоит 44.
- Кандидаты 0, 1 и 2 заказывают каждый день, 25 дней: 1100.
- Кандидаты 3, 5 и 7 заказывают через день, 13 дней: 572.
- Кандидат 6 заказывает раз в 3 дня, 9 дней: 396.
- Кандидат 4 заказывает раз в 4 дня, 7 дней: 308.

У кандидатов 0, 1 и 2 выходит на 500 с лишним больше, чем у тех, кто заказывает через день. Объёмы у них не лучше, и это не окупается.

**Кандидат 4.** Первая поставка приходит в день 5: 38 единиц товара 0 и 45 товара 1. Спрос за дни 5–8 по прогнозу — 72 и 86. Получается нехватка примерно 34 и 41 единицы, по 6 и 4 неустойки за каждую, плюс упущенная маржа. Длинный цикл приводит к крупным нехваткам.

**Кандидат 6.** Заказы примерно равны сумме прогноза за 3 дня. Например, приход в день 5 — 53/64 при спросе 48/58, приход в день 8 — 92/72 при спросе 92/78. Но средний множитель спроса около 1,046, так что план систематически отстаёт от фактического среднего примерно на 4–5 %. Остатки переходят на следующие дни, нехватки не переходят. Поэтому запас постепенно уходит вниз и растут неустойки. Каждая недостающая единица стоит около 12 (маржа плюс неустойка). Только систематическая недопоставка даёт около 50 единиц, это примерно 600. Ещё добавляются нехватки от разброса спроса. Экономия на постоянных затратах по сравнению с планом «через день» — всего 176. Кроме того, приход в день 8 почти упирается во вместимость склада 172.

**Кандидаты 3, 5 и 7** заказывают через день и различаются только запасом над прогнозом.
- Кандидат 7 (≈1,0× прогноза) повторяет проблему кандидата 6: заказы ниже фактического среднего спроса.
- Кандидат 5 (≈1,2× прогноза) даёт примерно 15 % лишнего сверх фактического среднего. Это около 100 с лишним единиц, которые будут списаны, при цене закупки 7–9 за штуку.
- Кандидат 3 (≈1,1× прогноза, то есть около 1,05× от фактического среднего) покрывает средний спрос с небольшим запасом против разброса. Годность 6 и 8 дней при цикле в 2 дня позволяет излишкам продаться в следующих периодах. Склад не переполняется: в день 9 на складе около 141 единицы при вместимости 172.

Кандидат 3 даёт лучший баланс между неустойками, списаниями и затратами на заказы.

I picked candidate 3. I worked this out in my head and did not simulate it, so treat it as a reasoned estimate.

- **How often to order:** ordering every second day beats ordering daily. Candidates 0–2 pay the 44 fee about 25 times (about 1,100 total). Candidates 3, 5 and 7 pay it about 13 times (about 570). That saves roughly 530. The extra holding cost from bigger batches is only about 240, so every-second-day ordering comes out about 290 ahead.
- **Why not bigger batches:** four-day batches (candidate 4) save another roughly 260 in fees. But they add about 460 in holding cost. Item 0 also lasts only 6 days, so more of it would go to waste. The 100 + 70 = 170 units arriving on day 9, plus stock already on hand, would likely overfill the 172-unit store and lose the excess. Candidate 6's three-day batches carry the same risks, only milder.
- **How much to order:** among the every-second-day plans, candidate 7 orders exactly the forecast. But actual demand averages about 4.6% above forecast. A missed sale (lost margin plus penalty) costs more than ordering one unit too many, so ordering a bit above forecast pays. Candidate 3 orders about 10% above forecast, which covers both. Candidate 5, at about 20% above, would mostly add unsold stock and holding cost.
- **Early shortages:** all plans run short on days 0–4 the same way. Only 27 units of item 0 are on hand against about 97 forecast demand, so this doesn't change the ranking.

**Ответ: кандидат 5.** Это оценка в уме по средним значениям, а не симуляция, поэтому выбор вероятный, но не гарантированный.

1. **Как часто заказывать.** Каждый день с заказом стоит 44. Планы 0–2 заказывают 25 дней подряд, это примерно 1100. Планы 3, 5 и 7 заказывают через день, около 13 раз, это примерно 572. Разница около 530 перевешивает почти любой другой выигрыш.
2. **Редкие крупные заказы упираются в склад.**
   - План 4 заказывает раз в 4 дня. Заказ дня 4 (100 + 70 = 170) приходит в день 9 при вместимости 172 и уже лежащих остатках. Значит, будет переполнение, и оплаченный товар пропадёт.
   - План 6 заказывает раз в 3 дня. Заказ дня 3 (92 + 72 = 164) приходит в день 8 с той же проблемой.
3. **Запас прочности среди 3, 5 и 7.** Двухдневный прогноз спроса покрывают: план 7 ровно (×1,0), план 3 с запасом ×1,09, план 5 с запасом ×1,2.
   - Нехватка дорогая: упущенная маржа плюс неустойка дают около 12 за единицу у обоих товаров.
   - Излишек дешёвый: хранение 0,7 и 0,2 в день, а срок годности 6 и 8 дней позволяет продать остаток на следующем цикле.
   - Средний множитель спроса 1,046, поэтому реальный запас у плана 5 около ×1,15, у плана 3 около ×1,04, а план 7 в среднем недозаказывает.
4. **Проверка склада для плана 5 в самый напряжённый день 9.** Приходит 80 + 60 = 140 единиц. Остаток от предыдущей поставки около 20–25. Итого примерно 160–165 из 172, то есть в среднем помещается. При низком спросе в дни 7–8 возможно небольшое переполнение. Но пропавшая единица стоит всего 7–9, это дешевле, чем нехватка у плана 3 или 7.

I'd pick **candidate 5**. I estimated this mentally rather than by running the plans, so the choice between candidates 5 and 3 is a judgement call.

1. **Order every second day.** Both goods take 5 days to arrive, and ordering costs 44 on any day you order. Daily ordering (candidates 0–2) pays this 25 times, about 1100. Ordering every second day (candidates 3, 5, 7) pays it 13 times, about 572. Holding an extra day's stock costs much less than the 528 saved.
2. **Drop the plans with large batches.** Candidate 4 orders every 4 days, so one delivery brings 170 units, and candidate 6 orders every 3 days, bringing 164. Add the stock already on the shelf and these go past the 172-unit warehouse limit, so the excess is lost.
3. **Choose the order size.**
   - Candidate 7 orders exactly the forecast (1.0×). But actual demand averages about 1.046× the forecast and varies a lot.
   - Running short costs a lot: about 12 per unit for either good (lost margin plus penalty). Overstock is cheaper. Leftovers can still be sold for 6 days (good 0) or 8 days (good 1), so a surplus mostly costs storage, plus some write-off of good 0.
   - That makes ordering above the forecast worthwhile. Candidate 3 orders about 1.1× and candidate 5 about 1.2×. Candidate 5 covers about 76% of the two-day demand spread, and its largest delivery (140 units on day 9) still fits in the warehouse.

I pick candidate 3: it orders every two days at about 1.1 × forecast. This is a rough comparison worked out without exact simulation.

1. **Order rhythm.** Each order day costs a fixed 44.
   - **Daily plans (0, 1, 2):** 25 order days cost 1100, about 530 more than ordering every two days. They save only about 9 per day in holding, roughly 225 over the period. That doesn't make up the 530.
   - **Every three days (6):** 9 order days save about 176. Average stock is about one day of demand, which adds about 9 per day in holding, roughly 225. So it ends up slightly worse.
   - **Every four days (4):** 7 order days save about 264. Average stock is about 1.5 days of demand, mostly product 0 at 0.7 per unit per day. That adds roughly 450 in holding. The delivery arriving on day 17 is 84 + 92 = 176 units against 172 of space, so at least 4 units are lost, plus whatever stock is left over. On day 9 it brings only 70 units of product 1, while demand over the next four days is about 82, so there are shortages.
   - **Every two days (3, 5, 7):** this is the best trade-off between fixed fees and holding.

2. **Order size within the two-day plans.** Average demand is about 1.046 × forecast, and over two days it varies by roughly 21%.
   - **Candidate 7 (≈1.0 × forecast):** it orders less than average demand, so it runs short often. Each missed unit of product 0 costs 12 (6 lost margin plus a 6 penalty).
   - **Candidate 5 (≈1.2 × forecast):** it builds a steady surplus of about 15% each cycle. Product 0 lasts only 6 days, so that surplus spoils at 7 per unit plus holding.
   - **Candidate 3 (≈1.1 × forecast):** it covers about the 60th percentile of demand. Since leftovers carry over to the next cycle, overstock is cheaper than a shortage, and this level balances the two best.

3. **Common to all plans.** The starting stock can't cover days 0–4 no matter what, so all candidates take the same shortage there. It doesn't change the ranking.

I recommend **candidate 3**. It is a 2‑day ordering cycle with order sizes about 10% above forecast, and it should give the highest expected profit. I worked this out by hand from rough estimates, without a step‑by‑step simulation, so treat it as a ranking, not exact profit figures.

1. **The first days are the same for every plan.** Orders take 5 days to arrive, so days 0–4 run only on starting stock. For product 0 that is 27 units against forecast demand of 97, which means shortages and penalties no matter which plan is chosen.

2. **Main trade‑off: order fees versus holding cost.** Each ordering day costs 44.
   - Daily orders (candidates 0, 1, 2) pay about 25 × 44 = 1,100.
   - Each extra day a unit waits costs about 210 per 30 days for product 0 and 65 for product 1, roughly 275 in total.
   - Ordering every k days, fees plus holding come to about 44·25/k + 275·(k−1):

   | Ordering cycle | Candidates | Fees + holding |
   |---|---|---|
   | Every day | 0, 1, 2 | ≈1,100 |
   | Every 2 days | 3, 5, 7 | ≈850 |
   | Every 3 days | 6 | ≈950 |
   | Every 4 days | 4 | ≈1,130 |

   Candidate 4 also has a capacity risk. Its batch of 170 units arriving on day 9 plus leftover stock can go over the 172‑unit limit, and the extra is lost.

3. **Order size within the 2‑day plans.** Average demand runs about 4.6% above forecast. Each unit short loses about 12 (6 lost margin + 6 penalty for product 0; 8 + 4 for product 1), while a surplus unit costs holding and sometimes a write‑off.
   - Candidate 7 orders exactly the forecast. It will run short on average and often in high‑demand days.
   - Candidate 5 orders about 20% above forecast. Because the plan is fixed, the surplus builds up and expires, especially product 0, which lasts only 6 days.
   - Candidate 3, at about 10% above forecast, covers average demand plus some of the randomness without much waste.

Candidate 3 also compares well with the best daily plan: candidate 0 orders a similar amount but pays about 528 more in order fees and saves only about 275 in holding.

I picked **candidate 3**. I worked this out by reasoning in my head, without simulating day by day, so the numbers below are estimates.

1. **Days 0–4 are the same for every plan.** No orders arrive before day 5, so all plans run short then. This doesn't separate the candidates.

2. **Fixed cost of 44 per order day.**
   - Daily ordering (candidates 0, 1, 2): 25 × 44 = 1100.
   - Every 2 days (candidates 3, 5, 7): 13 × 44 = 572.
   - Every 3 days (candidate 6): 396.
   - Every 4 days (candidate 4): 308.

   Daily ordering loses about 530 to the every-2-day plans just on this fee.

3. **Longer cycles mean more holding cost.** Each extra day in the cycle adds roughly 7 per day in holding for product 0 and about 2 per day for product 1. That is about 230 over the 30 days, which more than cancels the 176 saved by ordering every 3 days instead of every 2. Candidate 6 also risks overflowing the 172-unit warehouse on day 8 (164 units arrive on top of leftovers). Candidate 4 does worse still: its first order (38 and 45) is about half of the demand for days 5–8, which brings big shortages and penalties.

4. **Order size among the every-2-day plans.** Each of these plans orders a multiple of the forecast. Actual demand averages about 1.046 × forecast.
   - **Candidate 7 (1.0×):** it orders less than average demand, so it runs short regularly. Each lost unit costs about 12 (lost margin plus penalty).
   - **Candidate 5 (1.2×):** it orders about 15% more than demand. With fixed orders the surplus builds up, and holding product 0 at 0.7 per unit per day gets expensive. Some of the surplus also spoils or hits the 172-unit limit.
   - **Candidate 3 (1.1×):** it orders roughly what is actually needed plus a small buffer, so a single high-demand day is covered. When demand swings from the forecast, it is the most stable of the three.

Candidate 3 has the cheap ordering schedule, the lowest holding cost and the right order size, so it should have the highest expected profit.

**Ответ: кандидат 3.** Это оценка в уме, без симуляции. Главная неопределённость — кандидат 6, он отстаёт по прикидке всего примерно на 40.

1. **Ежедневные заказы (кандидаты 0, 1, 2)** проигрывают. Заказ в каждый из 25 дней стоит 25 × 44 = 1100 только на фиксированных платежах. При заказе через день это 13 × 44 = 572.
2. **Заказ раз в 4 дня (кандидат 4)** экономит на фиксированных платежах 572 − 308 = 264. Зато хранение растёт: лишний запас в среднем около одного дневного спроса, это примерно 19 × 0,7 + 20 × 0,2 ≈ 17 в день, или около 430 за 25 дней. Кроме того, поставки до 170 единиц плюс остатки упираются во вместимость склада 172, и часть товара пропадёт.
3. **Заказ раз в 3 дня (кандидат 6)** экономит 572 − 396 = 176 на фиксированных платежах. Лишний запас на хранении — около половины дневного спроса, это примерно 8,7 в день, или около 218 за период. Выходит примерно на 40 хуже, чем заказ через день, а крупные поставки вроде [92, 72] плюс остатки могут упереться во вместимость.
4. **Среди заказов через день (кандидаты 3, 5, 7)** различается только запас:
   - кандидат 7 заказывает ровно по прогнозу (×1,0), а средний множитель спроса 1,046, так что нехватка будет систематической;
   - кандидат 5 заказывает с запасом ×1,2, это примерно на 15 % выше среднего спроса, и излишки будут копиться и списываться;
   - кандидат 3 заказывает с запасом ×1,1, это чуть выше среднего спроса. Нехватка дорогая (упущенная маржа плюс неустойка), а остатки переходят на следующие дни (годность 6–8 дней), так что небольшой запас здесь выгоднее всего.

I chose **candidate 5**. I worked this through in my head with rough estimates and did not run a full simulation, so the choice is a judgement call, not an exact result.

1. **Days 1–4 are the same for every plan.** Orders take 5 days to arrive, so nothing comes in before day 5. Every plan runs short on these days in the same way, so they don't separate the candidates.
2. **Ordering every other day is cheaper.** A daily order costs 44 even when small. Candidates 0, 1 and 2 order every day and pay about 1,100 in order fees. Candidates 3, 5 and 7 order every other day and pay about 570. The roughly 530 difference outweighs what daily ordering gains in flexibility.
3. **Candidates 4 and 6 lose stock to bad sizing.**
   - **Candidate 4** orders every 4 days. Its day-0 order is 38 units of product 0, but forecast demand for days 5–8 is 72, so it runs out badly. Its day-4 order of 100 + 70 = 170 units arrives on top of leftover stock, close to the 172 limit, so some of it may overflow and be lost.
   - **Candidate 6** orders every 3 days. Its day-3 order of 92 + 72 = 164 units arrives on day 8, also on top of leftovers, so it may overflow. That order also undercovers product 1 at about 0.92 of forecast.
4. **Ordering above the forecast pays off.** Running short costs about 12 per unit for either product (lost margin plus the penalty). A surplus unit mostly sells in the next cycle, because product 0 keeps 6 days and product 1 keeps 8. An extra unit therefore costs mostly storage, roughly 1.4 per cycle for product 0. Actual demand also averages about 1.046 times the forecast, with a wide spread. That points to ordering about 1.15–1.2 times the forecast. Among the every-other-day plans:
   - Candidate 7 orders about 1.0 times forecast, which is too little.
   - Candidate 3 orders about 1.09 times forecast.
   - Candidate 5 orders about 1.2 times forecast. Its largest delivery, 140 units on day 9, plus leftovers stays under the 172 limit.

Candidate 5 is my best estimate. Candidate 3 is close behind.

I picked candidate 3. I reasoned this through by hand rather than simulating it step by step, so it's an estimate, not a certainty.

1. **Ordering fee (44 per day with any order).**
   - Candidates 0–2 order every day for 25 days: 1100.
   - Candidates 3, 5 and 7 order every other day, 13 times: 572.
   - Candidate 6 orders every third day, 9 times: 396.
   - Candidate 4 orders every fourth day, 7 times: 308.

2. **Holding versus ordering fees.** Larger batches mean more stock held overnight, and holding product 0 costs 0.7 per unit per day.
   - Going from daily to every other day saves about 22 a day in fees and adds only about 10–15 a day in holding. So candidates 0–2 lose roughly 400–500 to the every-other-day plans.
   - Every third day (candidate 6) saves another 176 in fees. But it adds about 9 a day of holding (half a day's extra demand: 20 × 0.7 + 21 × 0.2), which is about 225 over 25 days. The saving doesn't cover it.
   - Every fourth day (candidate 4) holds even more. Its first batch (38 and 45 units) is also well below demand for days 5–8 (72 and 86), so it starts with large shortages.

3. **Order size within the every-other-day plans.** I compared each order with forecast demand for the two days it covers.
   - Candidate 7 orders exactly the forecast. Average demand is about 1.046 times the forecast, so it runs short often. Each missed unit costs 12 (lost margin plus penalty).
   - Candidate 5 orders about 1.2 times the forecast, around 15% above average demand. The fixed plan can't correct for that, so the surplus builds up until the shelf life runs out. Each spoiled unit wastes about 7–9 in purchase cost, plus holding.
   - Candidate 3 orders about 1.1 times the forecast, just above average demand. That gives a small buffer against shortages without much spoilage, and it holds up best when real demand swings away from the forecast. Its batches also stay well under the 172-unit warehouse limit.

All plans lose sales on days 0–4 because the starting stock is too small. That hurts every candidate equally, so it doesn't change the ranking.

I pick **candidate 3**. I worked it out roughly in my head and didn't run a full day-by-day simulation, so this is an estimate.

**1. How often to order.** Every order day costs a fixed 44. Ordering less often saves on that fee but means holding more stock, and storage costs money.
- **Daily (candidates 0, 1, 2):** 25 order days × 44 = 1100 in fees, the most of any plan.
- **Every 2 days (3, 5, 7):** 572 in fees plus about 225 in storage, roughly 800 in total.
- **Every 3 days (6):** 396 in fees plus about 450 in storage, roughly 850.
- **Every 4 days (4):** 308 in fees plus about 675 in storage, roughly 980. Its deliveries (about 170 units) are also close to the 172-unit warehouse limit, so leftover stock plus a new delivery can overflow.

Ordering every 2 days comes out cheapest.

**2. How much to order (candidates 3, 5, 7).** The early shortage on days 0–4 is the same for every plan: the starting stock (27 and 38) can't cover demand, and the first orders only arrive on day 5. What separates these three is the order size compared with forecast demand:
- **Candidate 7** orders exactly the forecast. Actual demand averages about 1.046 × forecast, so stock keeps running short. Each missing unit costs 12 (lost margin plus penalty) for both products. That is the biggest loss.
- **Candidate 5** orders about 1.2 × forecast, so extra stock builds up steadily. For product 0, which costs 0.7 per unit per day to store, the storage bill reaches several hundred. Leftovers plus a large delivery also risk overflowing the warehouse.
- **Candidate 3** orders about 1.1 × forecast. That keeps a small safety buffer, which helps when demand comes in above forecast. Leftovers sell within their shelf life, so little is written off, and storage stays moderate.

Candidate 3 has the best expected profit and holds up best when actual demand differs from the forecast.

I pick **Candidate 3**, though with only moderate confidence. I worked this out by reasoning in my head, not by a full day-by-day simulation, so Candidate 6 or 5 could edge it out.

1. **Days 1–4 don't separate the candidates.** Every order takes 5 days to arrive, and the starting stock only covers about day 0. So every candidate runs short on days 1–4 and pays the same penalty there.

It adds roughly 230 in holding, because one day's worth of stock sits overnight. That leaves about 320 in favour of every second day.
3. **Ordering every 3–4 days runs into the 172-unit capacity.** Candidate 4's day-12 order is 84 + 92 = 176, so some of it is lost on arrival. Candidate 6's arrivals of about 164 on top of leftover stock could also go over 172. Its larger batches mean more holding, and it meets the day-9 spike of 54 with one big batch. These costs roughly cancel the 180 it saves in fees compared with every second day, so it carries more risk for little gain.
4. **How much extra to order.** A shortage costs about 12 per unit for either product (lost margin plus penalty). A surplus unit mostly carries over to later days, because the goods stay sellable for 6–8 days. That argues for ordering a bit above forecast, especially since actual demand averages about 1.046 × forecast.
   - Candidate 7 orders exactly the forecast, which is below the expected demand, so it runs short too often.
   - Candidate 5 orders about 1.2 × forecast. The fixed plan's surplus would build up and spoil, about 7 per unit of product 0, plus holding.
   - Candidate 3 orders about 1.1 × forecast. It keeps a small cushion that builds slowly and gets sold off oldest first.

I picked **candidate 3**. This comes from rough mental estimates, not a simulation, so the margin over the next-best options is small.

1. **How the plans differ.** An order placed on day t arrives on day t+5. Every plan sets each order from the forecast for the days that delivery covers. The plans differ in two ways: how often they order, and how many units they buy relative to the forecast.

2. **Daily plans (0, 1, 2) cost too much in fees.** Ordering every day means about 25 orders × 44 = 1100. Ordering every other day means about 13 orders, roughly 572. Ordering every other day does add some holding cost, about 0.5 day of demand held overnight. That is around 9 per day, or about 230 over the run. So every-other-day ordering comes out roughly 300 ahead of daily ordering.

3. **Every 3 days (plan 6) is close but slightly worse.** It has 9 orders, which saves about 176 in fees compared with every other day. But stock sits about half a day longer, which costs around 230 more in holding. Its large deliveries, such as 92 + 72 = 164 arriving on day 8, also come near the 172-unit capacity.

4. **Every 4 days (plan 4) is worse.** It saves about 264 in fees but adds about 460 in holding cost. Its first order also covers only 38 units of product 0 against about 72 units of forecast demand for days 5–8.

5. **Among the every-other-day plans (3, 5, 7), about 1.1× the forecast fits best.**
   - Demand runs on average 1.046× the forecast, and a missed sale is expensive (lost margin plus penalty). Unsold stock carries over for 6–8 days, so a buffer above the forecast pays off. That rules out plan 7, which orders exactly the forecast.
   - Plan 5 orders about 1.2× the forecast, so roughly 15% excess builds up each cycle and starts to spoil.
   - Plan 3 orders about 1.1× the forecast. That leaves a small buffer that grows slowly.

I picked **Candidate 3**. This is a rough mental estimate, not a full day-by-day simulation of each plan.

1. **Ordering cadence.** Each day with an order costs 44.
   - Daily plans (0, 1, 2) order on 25 days, so 1100 in fees.
   - Every-other-day plans (3, 5, 7) order on 13 days, so 572.
   - The every-3-days plan (6) orders on 9 days, so 396.
   - The every-4-days plan (4) orders on 7 days, so 308.

   Ordering every other day saves about 530 against daily ordering. It adds only about 150 in holding cost, because roughly half of each batch sits one extra night. Shelf life of 6 and 8 days easily covers a two-day batch. So plans 3, 5 and 7 should beat 0, 1 and 2.

2. **Longer cycles.**
   - **Plan 6:** saves another 176 in fees but adds about 225 in holding over the month. Its batches arrive at up to 164 units against a 172-unit warehouse. Any leftover stock pushes it over capacity, and the excess is lost. Its quantities also sit at roughly the forecast or below, while average demand is about 4.6% above forecast.
   - **Plan 4:** underorders clearly, for example 38/45 for days 5–8 against a forecast of 72/86, and 70 of product 1 against 82 needed for days 9–12. It also holds stock longer.

3. **Order size among 3, 5 and 7.** Running out costs the lost margin plus the penalty: 6+6=12 for product 0 and 8+4=12 for product 1. Leftover stock usually costs only holding, because it can be sold over the next few days before it expires. So it pays to order a little above average demand.
   - **Plan 7:** about 1.0× forecast, which is below average demand, so it runs short.
   - **Plan 5:** about 1.2× forecast. The surplus builds up and spoils.
   - **Plan 3:** about 1.09–1.12× forecast. That is a small buffer above average demand, which absorbs random swings without much spoilage.

That totals roughly 200 over the month, less than the ~530 saved on fees. Ordering every other day also lets the ups and downs of two days' demand partly cancel. So candidates 3, 5 and 7 come out ahead of the daily plans.

3. **Every 3 or 4 days is no better.**
   - Every 4 days (candidate 4) costs more in storage than it saves in fees. It also overflows the warehouse: the day 9 delivery of 100 + 70 = 170 units, on top of leftover stock, goes over the 172-unit limit and the excess is lost.
   - Every 3 days (candidate 6) roughly breaks even with every 2 days on fees plus storage. But its batch sizes are uneven: the delivery for days 8–10 covers only about 1.0× the forecast for product 0 and 0.92× for product 1. Large deliveries also push it close to the capacity limit.

4. **Order size: candidate 3 is closest to the best level.** A missing unit costs about 12 (lost margin plus penalty), while a leftover unit costs about 7–9 (purchase price plus storage). It therefore pays to order a bit above the expected demand. Expected demand is already about 1.05× the forecast, because the average random multiplier is 1.046.
   - Candidate 7 orders exactly the forecast (1.0×), which is too little.
   - Candidate 5 orders about 1.2×, which is too much.
   - Candidate 3 orders about 1.1×. For example, its day 0 order of 37 and 38 covers forecasts of 34 and 34 for days 5–6.

I chose **candidate 5**. I estimated this in my head without simulating the plans, so it's a reasoned estimate, not an exact calculation.

1. **How often to order.** Every order day costs 44, but bigger, rarer batches sit on the shelf longer and add storage cost. Product 0 costs 0.7 per unit per day to store and product 1 costs 0.2, with each selling about 20 units a day.
   - Ordering daily instead of every 2 days costs one extra 44 per 2 days but saves only about 18 in storage. So candidates 0, 1 and 2 lose.
   - Ordering every 3 days instead of every 2 saves 44 in fees per 6 days but adds about 54 in storage. So candidate 6 loses slightly.
   - Ordering every 4 days instead of every 2 saves about 264 in fees in total but adds about 430 in storage. Candidate 4 also overflows the 172-unit warehouse: the day-12 order alone is 84 + 92 = 176. It also under-orders in the first cycles.
   - So ordering every 2 days is best, which leaves candidates 3, 5 and 7.

2. **How much to order.** These three differ only in quantity. Candidate 7 orders exactly the forecast, candidate 3 about 1.1 times it, and candidate 5 about 1.2 times it.
   - Real demand averages about 1.046 times the forecast and swings by roughly ±30% a day.
   - A missing unit costs about 12 for either product (lost margin plus the shortage penalty).
   - A spare unit usually just carries over to the next delivery, because product 0 keeps 6 days and product 1 keeps 8. So it costs only about 1.4 or less in storage.
   - With shortages costing far more than spares, ordering above the forecast pays off, so the largest buffer (about 1.2 times) wins.

3. **Warehouse capacity.** Candidate 5's largest delivery (day 9) is 140 units. Even with about 20 units left over from earlier, that's around 160, so it fits in 172.

**Выбор: кандидат 3.** Оценка сделана в уме и приблизительно. Ближайший соперник — кандидат 6; по моей оценке, кандидат 3 впереди примерно на 50, и эту разницу я считаю неуверенной.

**Как устроены планы.** Заказ дня t покрывает спрос со дня t + 5. Кандидаты различаются частотой заказов и запасом сверх прогноза.

**Затраты на заказы и хранение.** Сравнивал с кандидатом 3, заказы раз в 2 дня:

| Частота заказов | Кандидаты | Плата за дни заказа | Хранение, примерно | Итог против кандидата 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Каждый день | 0, 1, 2 | 25 × 44 = 1100 | почти ноль | Сверх 572 платится 528, на хранении экономится лишь около 225. Хуже. |
| Раз в 2 дня | 3, 5, 7 | 13 × 44 = 572 | около 9 в день | База для сравнения. |
| Раз в 3 дня | 6 | 9 × 44 = 396 | около 18 в день | На заказах экономится 176, на хранении теряется около 225. Немного хуже. |
| Раз в 4 дня | 4 | 7 × 44 = 308 | около 27 в день | На заказах экономится 264, на хранении теряется около 450. Хуже. |

У кандидата 4 есть и другие проблемы:
- **Заказы по прогнозу ниже спроса.** Партия дня 4 по товару 1 покрывает около 85 % прогноза, партия дня 8 по товару 0 — около 88 %.
- **Склад переполняется.** Партия 84 + 92 = 176, приходящая в день 17, больше вместимости 172, поэтому часть товара пропадает ещё до учёта остатков.

**Запас сверх прогноза в группе «раз в 2 дня».** Средний спрос равен 1,046 × прогноз. Потеря от нехватки — примерно 12 за единицу: упущенная маржа плюс неустойка. Небольшой излишек почти ничего не стоит: из-за срока годности он продаётся в следующей партии, платится только хранение. Систематический излишек копится и списывается.
- **Кандидат 7** заказывает 1,0 × прогноз. Это ниже среднего спроса, поэтому нехватка будет постоянной.
- **Кандидат 5** заказывает около 1,2 × прогноз, то есть примерно на 15 % больше среднего спроса. Списания и хранение будут большими.
- **Кандидат 3** заказывает около 1,09–1,1 × прогноз, примерно на 4 % больше среднего. Этого хватает на небольшой страховой запас без заметных списаний. Его крупнейшая поставка, 75 + 56 = 131, далеко от лимита склада.

**Устойчивость.** При случайном спросе у кандидата 3 есть небольшой запас, а частые и умеренные поставки быстро гасят отклонения.

**Ответ: кандидат 3.** Считал в уме, на средних значениях, без моделирования, так что разрыв между лучшими планами оценён грубо. Кандидат 3 впереди, но небольшой.

**Как устроены планы.** Заказ дня t приходит в день t+5 и закрывает спрос следующих дней. Спрос дней 0–4 одинаково не покрыт у всех: до дня 5 ничего не приходит, а стартового запаса товара 0 (27) не хватает. Поэтому планы различаются двумя вещами:
- **Как часто заказывать.** Каждый день: 25 дней заказа × 44 = 1100. Через день: 13 × 44 = 572. Раз в 3 дня: 9 × 44 = 396. Раз в 4 дня: 7 × 44 = 308.
- **Какой запас сверх прогноза.** Средний множитель спроса около 1,046. Остатки не пропадают сразу: товар 0 годен 6 дней, товар 1 — 8 дней. Нехватка стоит дорого: у товара 0 это 12 (6 недополученной маржи + 6 неустойки), у товара 1 — 12 (8 + 4). Лишняя единица до продажи стоит только хранения. Поэтому запас около ×1,1 к прогнозу разумен. Заказ ровно по прогнозу (×1,0) систематически недобирает. При ×1,2 лишний товар копится и списывается: примерно 4 ед./день на 7–9 за единицу.

**Сравнение:**
- **Кандидаты 0, 1, 2** (заказ каждый день). Платят примерно на 530 больше за дни заказа, чем двухдневные планы, а экономят на хранении только около 200. У кандидата 2 к тому же заказ ×1,0, то есть хроническая нехватка.
- **Кандидат 4** (раз в 4 дня). Заказ дня 0 (38 ед. товара 0) приходит в день 5 и должен покрыть дни 5–8 со спросом около 72. Это около 34 ед. нехватки по 12 за единицу. Кроме того, хранение на 4 дня дорогое, а приход 170 ед. почти упирается во вместимость 172 — при случайном спросе излишек пропадёт.
- **Кандидат 6** (раз в 3 дня). По сравнению с двухдневным планом экономит 176 на днях заказа, но хранение дороже примерно на 8,75 в день, около 210 за период. Заказ дня 3 (92 и 72) ограничен вместимостью склада и не имеет запаса на всплеск спроса 54 в день 9. Итог немного хуже кандидата 3.
- **Кандидаты 7, 3, 5** (через день). Различаются только запасом: ×1,0, ×1,1 и ×1,2. У 7 нехватка, у 5 списания и лишнее хранение. Кандидат 3 с запасом ×1,1 устойчивее к отклонениям спроса в обе стороны.
